title: Functions
summary: Put a repeatable piece of work into a **method**.
refresher: Java calls functions methods. A method has a name, a **return type**, and optional **parameters**. `void` means it does not **return** a value. A non-void method must return the kind of value it promised.

sections.title: Read a method signature
sections.summary: Name reusable work and identify the **return type**, name, and **parameters**.

blocks.body: Java calls a **function** a **method**. Same idea, different word. A method gives a name to a piece of work so you can use it again without copying the same lines all over your program.

blocks.caption: Before real syntax, learn the shape: a **function** has a name, inputs, a body, and sometimes a returned result. The examples after this show the exact syntax.
blocks.code:
function name(parameters):
    body that does the job
    return the result

call function name(arguments)

blocks.title: Follow a function call
blocks.caption: See arguments enter a function, a local variable appear, and return send the answer back.

steps.title: Call with arguments
steps.body: The caller sends 3 and 5 into the function.

steps.title: Parameters receive values
steps.body: Inside the function, a is 3 and b is 5.

function_flow.arguments: 3 goes to a, 5 goes to b

steps.title: Return
steps.body: Return sends 8 back to the caller, and the function call is finished.

steps.title: Caller resumes
steps.body: The method call has been replaced by 8, so main can use the stored result.

blocks.caption: Notice that defining and running are two different events. The body of `greet` sits there inert until `main` says its name. Here `main` says it twice, and only then does anything appear on screen.
blocks.output:
Welcome to Morgan State.
Welcome to Morgan State.
blocks.body: The first line of a **method** tells Java how the method can be used. The **return type** says what comes back. The name says what to call. The parentheses hold the **values** the method needs from you.

The first line of a **method** is its signature. It tells Java who can call the method, whether it is `static`, what it returns, its name, and its **parameters**. The rest of this lesson shows only methods; imagine the usual `class Main` wrapper around them.
blocks.caption: This **method** takes a name and returns a greeting. It does not **print** by itself; it hands the **String** back to the caller.

blocks.title: Reading a signature left to right
items: `public` is the modifier: who is allowed to call this **method**.
`static` means the **method** belongs to the **class** itself, not to an **object** built from it.
`int` is the **return type**: the kind of **value** `return` sends back. Use `void` when nothing does.
`doubled` is the name. Java style is a verb in camelCase, so `calculateGpa`, not `calculate_gpa`.
`(int n)` is the **parameter list**: what the **method** needs, and the type of each thing it needs.
blocks.body: `return` and `System.out.println` are not the same. Printing shows a **value** to a person. Returning gives a value back to the program so another line can use it.

blocks.caption: You will see `static` a lot in beginner Java because `main` is static. For now, read a static **method** as one you can call from main without building an **object** first.

sections.title: Match arguments to typed parameters
sections.summary: A method call fills typed **parameters** by position.

blocks.body: Java checks method calls against the method signature. The caller supplies arguments, and Java matches them to parameters from left to right.

blocks.caption: The call sends `7` into `score` and `3` into `bonus`. The names in the call do not have to match the parameter names.

blocks.title: Types are part of the promise
blocks.body: If a method says `int score`, the call must provide a value Java can use as an integer. The method body can trust that shape once the code compiles.

blocks.code: static int addBonus(int score, int bonus)
blocks.why: Arguments match parameters by position, so the second argument fills the second parameter.

sections.title: Return vs println
sections.summary: Distinguish showing **output** from giving the caller a usable **value**.

blocks.body: Printing is for a human reading the screen. `return` is for code that needs to use the value later. Once a value is only printed, your program cannot grab it back.

blocks.caption: Where `println` throws a **value** away after showing it, `return` delivers it to whoever made the call. Delivered means usable, so you can assign it, add it, or pass it onward. Watch the final line: since `doubled` yields an `int`, two calls can be summed on the spot, giving 6 plus 8.

blocks.title: println shows a value. return gives a value back.
blocks.body: `System.out.println` sends text to the screen. `return` sends a **value** back to the caller. Use return when another line of code needs the answer.

blocks.caption: Both versions can show 10 on screen. Only the right version returns a value the caller can store and use. The left version is `void`, so it cannot be assigned to `answer`.

blocks.prompt: What happens when you try to run this?
choices: It does not compile, because a void method gives back no value to store in `answer`
It compiles and prints 16 once, and `answer` is quietly left at 0
blocks.why: Typed `void`, `square` yields nothing, yet `int answer = square(4);` tries to park that nothing inside an `int`. Javac throws the **file** out with "incompatible types: void cannot be converted to int", so execution never begins and 16 is never printed. Choosing "prints 16, then prints null" is Python thinking: over there, a **function** lacking a **return** slips back `None` and the program carries on. Java declines to start at all. Switch `void` to `int`, turn `System.out.println(n * n)` into `return n * n`, and it will build.

sections.title: Every path must return
sections.summary: Make non-void **methods** deliver the promised type on every route.

blocks.title: Every path has to reach a return
blocks.body: If a method promises to return an `int`, every path through the method must return an int. If one path can fall out the bottom, Java reports `missing return statement`.

blocks.caption: Both **branches** return a **value**, so Java is satisfied. If you remove the else, one possible path has no return, and Java refuses to compile it.

blocks.body: A `static` **method** belongs to the **class**. A non-static method belongs to an **object**. Because `main` is static, it can call other static methods directly, but it needs an object before calling non-static ones.

sections.title: Static calls and local scope
sections.summary: Understand why beginner **methods** are static and why local **variables** stay inside a method.

blocks.caption: One word separates these: `static` on the **method**. Javac throws out the left one with "non-static method triple(int) cannot be referenced from a static context". Unpacked, that sentence means `main` is static, so whatever it calls by bare name has to be static as well.

A **variable** declared inside a method only exists inside that method. That region is its **scope**. If `main` tries to use a variable created inside `shout`, Java reports `cannot find symbol`, and the program does not run.

blocks.prompt: This **method** is supposed to give back the larger of two numbers. What does javac do with it?
choices: It refuses to compile, because one path through the method returns nothing
It compiles, then crashes at runtime with a NullPointerException
blocks.why: An `int` was promised, but should `a > b` turn out false, control slides to the closing brace with nothing delivered. Javac refuses that and reports "missing **return** statement", so the program never launches. Picking "compiles, runs, and prints 9" is the Python reflex, where the identical shape runs fine and slips back `None`. Java audits all routes before producing a **class** **file**. Drop `return b;` underneath the `if` and it builds, and at that point 9 is indeed what you see.

blocks.title: Before you call a method done
items: Use **return** when the program needs the answer back.
Use void only when there is no answer to **return**.
Match the returned **value** to the promised **return type**.

call-01.title: Definition is not execution
call-01.body: A function or method body waits until code calls it.
call-01.notice: Find the actual call before expecting the body to run.
call-01.mistake: Do not count a function body just because it appears above the output line.

print-not-return-01.title: Printing is not returning
print-not-return-01.body: Printing shows a value to the person. Returning hands a value back to the program.
print-not-return-01.notice: Check whether the function has a return value or only output side effects.
print-not-return-01.mistake: Do not store the result of a no-return function and expect a useful value instead of nothing from void.

return-value-01.title: Returned values replace the call
return-value-01.body: A function call with a return value can be used inside a larger expression.
return-value-01.notice: Evaluate each call, replace it with its returned value, then finish the expression.
return-value-01.mistake: Do not ignore the returned value when the next line uses it.

return-stops-01.title: Return exits immediately
return-stops-01.body: Once a return statement runs, the rest of that function call is over.
return-stops-01.notice: After an early return, skip later lines in the same function call.
return-stops-01.mistake: Do not keep executing a function after it has already returned.

missing-return-01.title: Every path needs a return plan
missing-return-01.body: If one branch returns but another branch reaches the end, the function may hand back no useful value.
missing-return-01.notice: Trace the path for the specific input, not only the branch that looks intended.
missing-return-01.mistake: Do not assume a skipped branch magically returns the other argument.

arg-order-01.title: Arguments fill parameters by position
arg-order-01.body: The first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second, and so on unless named arguments are used.
arg-order-01.notice: Write the parameter values before evaluating the body.
arg-order-01.mistake: Do not swap argument meaning because the names would sound nicer the other way.

local-scope-01.title: Local variables stay inside
local-scope-01.body: A value created inside a function or method is not automatically available outside it.
local-scope-01.notice: Use return values to move information out of a function.
local-scope-01.mistake: Do not print an inside-only name after the function has finished.

reuse-01.title: Each call runs fresh
reuse-01.body: Calling the same function more than once applies the same rule to new arguments.
reuse-01.notice: Evaluate each call separately, then combine the returned values.
reuse-01.mistake: Do not reuse the previous call's local parameter values.

function-in-condition-01.title: Boolean functions can drive decisions
function-in-condition-01.body: A function that returns true or false can be used directly as a condition.
function-in-condition-01.notice: Evaluate the returned boolean before choosing the branch.
function-in-condition-01.mistake: Do not print the boolean if the code uses it to choose an if or else path.

param-copy-01.title: Changing a parameter may not change the caller
param-copy-01.body: A parameter is the function's local name for the value it received.
param-copy-01.notice: If the function returns an updated value, the caller must store that return to keep it.
param-copy-01.mistake: Do not assume a local parameter assignment rewrites the original variable.
